item.research_question: Can a dual molecular precursor approach using MoL4 and WS(S2)L2 rapidly produce ternary layered metal chalcogenide (Mo1–xWxS2) and oxide (Mo1–xWxO3) alloys with controlled stoichiometry at low temperatures?
item.material_system: Mo1–xWxS2 and Mo1–xWxO3 alloys with nominal stoichiometries x = 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.0
item.processing_route: Thermolysis of molecular precursors MoL4 and WS(S2)L2 in a tube furnace for 1 h at 450 °C under argon flow (300 sccm) for sulfides, or at 500 °C in air for oxides
item.test_conditions: Characterization performed using Raman spectroscopy (488 nm laser), powder X-ray diffraction (Cu Kα), XPS (Al Kα), SEM-EDX (1–1.5 kV SE, 30 kV EDX), and STEM-EDX (200–300 kV)
key_findings: Sulfide alloys (Mo1–xWxS2) adopt the 2H-hexagonal layered structure of MoS2, with no significant diffraction from (002) planes indicating ultrathin/nanoscale nature.
Oxide alloys (Mo1–xWxO3) with 0.25 ≤ x ≤ 0.75 comprise a mixture of three related WO3 structures (orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic) and varying amounts of α-MoO3.
Raman E2g1 mode shifts from 381 cm⁻¹ (MoS2) to 375 cm⁻¹ (Mo0.25W0.75S2) and 353 cm⁻¹ (WS2), while A1g shifts from 403 cm⁻¹ to 408 cm⁻¹ with increasing W content.
STEM-EDX mapping confirms uniform elemental distribution of Mo, W, S, and O at the nanoscale, with quantification matching expected Cliff Lorimer ratios.
Sulfide nanomaterials consist of two populations: nanoparticles (3–9 nm diameter) and nanosheets (5–17 nm lateral size, <3 atomic layers thickness).
Oxide nanomaterials consist of roughly spherical nanoparticles with mean sizes between 3 and 5 nm, consistent with the less anisotropic WO3 crystal structure.
XPS analysis shows Mo4+ binding energy shifts from 230.7 to 230.4 eV as W content increases to 75%, attributed to increased electron attraction by W.
The oxide system is described as a paracrystal with varying short-to-medium local order governed by the tilt angle of MO6 octahedra induced by strain.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the molecular precursors codecompose at the molecular scale, allowing for excellent control of dopant homogeneity. In the oxide system, the formation of multiple interrelated phases (orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic) is attributed to strain-induced variations in the tilt angle of MO6 octahedra, resulting in a paracrystalline structure rather than a single thermodynamic phase.
item.limitations: The sensitivity of the samples to damage by the high-energy STEM electron probe prevents compositional analysis at the atomic scale.
item.future_work: The authors state that the new synthetic pathway allows access to potentially interesting metastable structures, implying future work could explore these specific metastable phases and their properties.
quotes: Either transition-metal dichalcogenides or transition-metal oxides can be produced from the same pair of precursors by the choice of reaction conditions
The variations in the crystal structure away from the parent monoclinic WO3 structure are strain-induced; as the amount of Mo is reduced, the amount of monoclinic structure is increased.
This approach represents a step change in producing ternary transition-metal dichalcogenide alloys at a fraction of the time compared to traditional solid-state reactions
